tool.name: Zapier
tool.tagline: Connect thousands of apps with no-code automations (Zaps), AI steps and MCP
tool.description: Zapier is a no-code automation service: you build Zaps, small workflows where an event in one app (a new form entry, a new email) makes things happen in other apps. It connects more than 9,000 apps, stores data in Tables, collects input with Forms, and adds AI steps that can read, write and use your apps as tools. It is the quickest way for non-programmers to remove repetitive copy-and-paste work.

concepts.name: What Zapier is: Zaps, triggers and actions
concepts.summary: Understand the core idea: a Zap watches for an event in one app and then does things in other apps for you.
concepts.why: Every other Zapier feature is built on this one picture, so getting it clear first makes the rest easy.
concepts.body:
Think of a chore you do by hand: every time someone fills in your website form, you copy their name and email into a spreadsheet and send them a welcome email. Zapier does that chore for you, every time, without you being there.

The automation is called a **Zap**. A Zap is a small recipe with two kinds of steps:

- A **trigger**: the event that starts the Zap. "When a new form entry arrives" or "when a new email lands in Gmail".
- One or more **actions**: what Zapier does after the trigger. "Add a row to Google Sheets", "send a Slack message".

Each step talks to an **app** (a service such as Gmail, Slack or HubSpot). Zapier connects to more than 9,000 apps, and it also has built-in helper apps whose names end in "by Zapier", such as Formatter by Zapier or Webhooks by Zapier.

Every time the trigger event happens, the Zap **runs** once from top to bottom. That one run is logged in your history, and each action that succeeds normally counts as one **task**, the unit Zapier uses to measure how much you automate.

Building a Zap always follows the same three moves: build it (choose apps and events, fill in the fields), test each step, then publish it so it starts running on new events. A published Zap only reacts to things that happen after you publish it, not to old data.

Beyond Zaps, Zapier offers Tables (a simple database), Forms (simple pages and forms), Canvas (a whiteboard for mapping processes), AI steps, and MCP, a way for AI assistants to use your apps. This course covers all of them, starting with Zaps.
takeaways: A Zap = one trigger + one or more actions
Each time the trigger fires, the Zap runs once and successful actions usually count as tasks
Build, test, publish: a published Zap only handles new events
pitfalls: Expecting a new Zap to process old emails or rows that existed before it was published.

quiz.q: In the Zap "When a new Typeform entry arrives, add a row to Google Sheets", what is the trigger?
options: Adding a row to Google Sheets
quiz.explain: The trigger is the event that starts the Zap; adding the row is the action.

concepts.name: Apps and app connections
concepts.summary: Connect your accounts (Gmail, Slack, a CRM) to Zapier once, then reuse those connections in any Zap.
concepts.why: A Zap can only read or change data in an app after you have given Zapier safe, limited permission to that account.
concepts.body:
Before Zapier can read your Gmail or post in your Slack, you must give it permission. You do this once per account by creating an **app connection** (a saved, secure link between Zapier and one of your accounts).

When you add an app to a Zap, Zapier asks you to sign in to that app. Two common ways this works:

- **OAuth**: a pop-up from the app itself (for example Google) asks "Allow Zapier to access your account?". You never give Zapier your password; the app hands Zapier a permission slip instead.
- **API key**: some apps instead give you a long secret code in their settings. An API key is like a password for programs, so you paste it into Zapier and keep it private.

Zapier stores these credentials (the login details) encrypted, and a connection only allows what that account is permitted to do. If your account cannot delete records in the CRM, neither can your Zap.

One connection can be reused in many Zaps. Give connections clear names such as "Gmail - Support inbox" so you pick the right one later, and remove ones you no longer use.

Connections sometimes **expire** or break: you changed your password, your company added new security rules, or the account lost permissions. Zaps that use a broken connection start failing until you reconnect it from the app connections page.

On team accounts you can **share** a connection with colleagues so they can build Zaps with it without knowing the password, and administrators can control which apps people are allowed to connect.
takeaways: An app connection is Zapier's saved, encrypted permission to use one of your accounts
OAuth means signing in through the app; an API key is a secret code you paste in
Name connections clearly and reconnect them when they expire
pitfalls: Building an important team Zap on a personal account connection that breaks when that person leaves.

quiz.q: Your Zaps that post to Slack suddenly fail after you changed your Slack password. What is the most likely fix?
quiz.explain: Password changes often invalidate a saved connection; reconnecting it fixes every Zap that uses it.

concepts.name: Triggers: instant and polling
concepts.summary: Learn how a trigger notices new events, why some Zaps start within seconds and others after a few minutes.
concepts.why: Knowing how your trigger checks for new data explains most "why didn't my Zap run yet?" questions.
concepts.body:
A trigger is the "when" of a Zap. Zapier notices new events in one of two ways.

**Polling triggers** work like checking your mailbox on a timer. Every few minutes Zapier asks the app, "anything new since last time?". If yes, the Zap runs once for each new item. How often Zapier checks depends on your plan, so a polling Zap can start a few minutes after the event.

**Instant triggers** work like a doorbell. The app itself tells Zapier the moment something happens, so the Zap starts within seconds. In the editor these are marked "Instant".

Most triggers are about something new: "New Row", "New Email Matching Search", "New Deal". Some are about changes: "Updated Row". Read the trigger description carefully, because "new" usually means created after the Zap was published, and "updated" may fire more often than you expect.

Zapier keeps track of which items it has already seen, so the same item normally does not start the Zap twice.

When you test a trigger, Zapier pulls a few recent sample items from the app. These samples are only for setting up later steps; picking one does not run your Zap for real.

For polling Zaps you can also click a button in the editor to check for new data right away instead of waiting. And if no app trigger fits, built-in triggers such as Schedule by Zapier (run every day at 9:00) or Webhooks by Zapier (run when another system calls a special web address) can start a Zap. Those come later in the course.
takeaways: Polling triggers check on a timer; instant triggers are notified right away
Test samples help you build, they don't run the Zap
"New" and "updated" triggers behave differently: read the description

quiz.q: A Zap with a polling trigger ran 6 minutes after a new row was added. What does this most likely mean?
options: Zapier checked for new data on its normal timer
quiz.explain: Polling triggers look for new items at intervals, so a delay of a few minutes is expected.

concepts.name: Actions, searches and multi-step Zaps
concepts.summary: Chain several actions in one Zap, and use search actions to find existing records before you create or update them.
concepts.why: Real processes have several steps; one Zap with many steps is easier to manage than many tiny Zaps.
concepts.body:
After the trigger you can add as many action steps as you need. They run in order, top to bottom, every time the Zap runs.

Example: when a new order arrives in your shop,

- 1. Trigger: New Order in Shopify
- 2. Action: Create Contact in your email marketing app
- 3. Action: Add Row in Google Sheets
- 4. Action: Send Channel Message in Slack

Actions come in a few flavours:

- **Create** actions add something new (a contact, a task, a row).
- **Update** actions change something that already exists, so they need to know which record (usually by its ID, a unique number or code the app gives each record).
- **Search** actions ("Find Contact", "Lookup Spreadsheet Row") look for an existing record. Many have an option to create the record if nothing is found, which prevents duplicates.

A common pattern is search, then update: find the customer by email, then update that customer. Without the search you would create a new duplicate customer every time.

Each step needs its own app connection and its own settings. A Zap can hold up to 100 steps, but long Zaps are harder to read and test. If a group of steps is reused by several Zaps, later lessons show how to package it as a Sub-Zap.

Every action step that succeeds normally counts as one task. Built-in logic steps such as filters and paths do not.
takeaways: Actions run in order after the trigger
Use a search action before update actions to avoid duplicates
Each successful action usually uses one task
pitfalls: Using "Create" where a record may already exist, which fills your CRM with duplicates.

quiz.q: You want to update an existing customer when they place a new order. Which step usually comes first?
quiz.explain: You need to find the existing record (and its ID) before an update action can change it.

concepts.name: Mapping data between steps
concepts.summary: Insert values from earlier steps (a name, an email, an order total) into later steps so each run uses its own data.
concepts.why: Mapping is what turns a fixed message into a personalised one; nearly every Zap depends on it.
concepts.body:
Every step produces **data**: a set of named values called **fields**. A new form entry might produce the fields `name`, `email` and `plan`. Behind the scenes Zapier receives this as **JSON**, a common text format that writes data as `"field name": value` pairs inside curly braces, like the example below. You never have to type JSON yourself; it just helps to recognise it.

**Mapping** means filling a field in a later step with a value from an earlier step. In the action's field box, type `/` or click the insert button, pick the earlier step, then pick the field. It appears as a small coloured pill such as "1. Email".

The pill is a placeholder. On each run Zapier swaps it for that run's real value. If you typed `ana@example.com` by hand instead, every run would send to Ana.

You can mix fixed text and pills: `Welcome, [1. Name]! Your plan: [1. Plan]`.

Some data is **nested** (a field inside a field, like the address inside the customer). Zapier shows nested fields with names such as "Customer Address City".

Lists of things, such as the products in one order, are called **line items**. Mapping a line-item field into a normal text box joins all values with commas. Later lessons show how to loop over line items instead.

Tip: test the trigger with a realistic sample. The fields you can map come from the sample, and a field that was empty in the sample may be hidden from the list.
takeaways: Fields from earlier steps can be mapped into later steps as placeholders
Mapped values change on every run; typed values stay fixed
Nested fields and line items need a little extra care
pitfalls: Typing a sample value by hand instead of mapping the field, so every run uses the same value.

quiz.q: Your Zap sends every welcome email to the same person. What is the likely cause?
options: The email address was typed in instead of mapped from the trigger
The Zap has too many steps
quiz.explain: A typed value is fixed; a mapped field is replaced by each run's own data.

concepts.name: Testing, drafts, publishing and versions
concepts.summary: Test each step before going live, edit a published Zap safely as a draft, and roll back to an earlier version.
concepts.why: Testing catches mistakes before they touch real customers, and drafts let you change a live Zap without stopping it.
concepts.body:
Each step in the editor has a **Test** button. Testing the trigger fetches sample data. Testing an action really performs it once with that sample: a test email is actually sent, a test row is actually added. So test with harmless data, or point actions at a test spreadsheet or your own inbox first.

Test results show exactly what the app returned. If a step fails here, the error message usually names the problem: a missing required field, a wrong format, or a permission issue.

When everything works, click **Publish**. The Zap turns on and handles new events from then on.

Changing a live Zap does not interrupt it. Your edits go into a **draft**, while the published version keeps running. When you publish the draft, it replaces the live Zap. There is only one draft at a time, and deleting a draft leaves the live Zap unchanged.

Every publish creates a numbered **version** that you can name, such as "v4 - added Slack alert". Run history shows which version handled each run. If a change goes wrong, you can start a new draft from an older version and publish it, which works as a rollback. How long versions are kept depends on your plan.

Good habits:

- Name each Zap after what it does: "New Shopify order -> CRM + Slack".
- Turn the Zap on, then create one real event and check the result yourself.
- Keep related Zaps in folders.
takeaways: Testing an action really performs it, so use safe test data
Edits to a live Zap go into a draft until you publish
Each publish creates a version you can roll back to
pitfalls: Testing a "Send Email" action against a real customer list.

quiz.q: You edit a published Zap but haven't published the changes yet. What runs when a new event arrives?
options: Nothing, the Zap is paused while editing
quiz.explain: Drafts don't affect the live Zap; the published version keeps running until you publish the draft.

concepts.name: Zap history, run statuses and tasks
concepts.summary: Use Zap history to see every run, what data went through each step, and why something stopped or failed.
concepts.why: When someone asks "did the automation run?", Zap history is where you find the answer.
concepts.body:
**Zap history** is the logbook of your automations. Every run is listed with its time, its Zap and its **status**. Open a run to see each step's input data (what went in) and output data (what came back).

Common statuses:

- **Success**: every step that should run did run.
- **Filtered**: a filter step stopped the run on purpose (covered in the filters lesson). Nothing is wrong.
- **Errored**: a step failed, for example the app rejected the data.
- **Held**, **Waiting** or **Delayed**: the run is paused, for example by a Delay step or while waiting for an approval.
- **Stopped** or halted: the run ended early, for example because a step had nothing to do.

You can filter history by date, Zap, app, folder, owner and status, and search it. You can also open runs from inside the Zap editor while you build.

The history page also shows **task usage**. Most successful action steps use one task; some steps use more, such as Code steps with a longer runtime or AI steps with tools. Filters and paths themselves use none.

Unsuccessful runs can be **replayed** (run again), which the error-handling lesson covers.

History is not an archive: Zapier only guarantees about 60 days of run data. If you need long-term records, for example for an audit, export the history regularly or have the Zap also write a log row to a table.
takeaways: Zap history shows every run with each step's input and output
Filtered is not an error; errored is
Run data is kept for a limited time: export it if you need records

quiz.q: A run shows the status "Filtered". What happened?
options: A filter step intentionally stopped the run
quiz.explain: Filtered means the data did not meet a filter's conditions, so the remaining steps were skipped by design.

concepts.name: AI by Zapier steps: prompts and output fields
concepts.summary: Add an AI step that summarises, classifies, extracts or writes text, and returns named fields for later steps.
concepts.why: AI steps let a Zap handle messy text (emails, notes, reviews) that fixed rules can't understand.
concepts.body:
**AI by Zapier** is a built-in app that adds an AI step to any Zap. Inside it, a large language model (the kind of AI behind chat assistants) reads text from earlier steps and does what your prompt asks.

The step has two panels. In **Configure** you write the **prompt** (your instructions to the model). Type `/` to insert fields from earlier steps, such as the email body. Templates exist for four common jobs: Summarize, Write, Classify and Extract.

Then you define **output fields**: the named results you want back, each with a type and an optional description. Example for support emails:

- `category` (text): one of Billing, Bug, Question
- `urgent` (true/false)
- `summary` (text): one sentence

Because the answer comes back as separate fields, later steps can map them, or a filter can check `urgent`. This is far more reliable than asking for one paragraph and hoping. You can also have Zapier suggest fields from your prompt.

In the **Preview** panel you test the step on sample data before saving.

You choose a model tier (Standard, Advanced, Premium) or connect your own AI provider account. Stronger tiers use more tasks per run, so pick the simplest tier that does the job well. Specific model names change often; the tier list in the editor is the current reference.

AI output can be wrong or invented (a hallucination). Keep the step's job narrow, list allowed values, and check results in Zap history before trusting it fully.
takeaways: An AI by Zapier step = a prompt with mapped data + output fields
Output fields turn free text into values later steps can use
Pick the simplest model tier that works, and check results
pitfalls: Asking for one long free-text answer and then trying to split it in later steps instead of defining output fields.

quiz.q: Why define an output field "category" with allowed values rather than asking the AI to "describe the email"?
options: It removes the need for a prompt
Later steps and filters can rely on a predictable value
It makes the AI never wrong
quiz.explain: A named field with known values can be mapped and checked; a free description can't be relied on.

concepts.name: Filters: only continue when it matters
concepts.summary: Add a filter step that lets a run continue only when the data meets your conditions.
concepts.why: Filters stop Zaps from acting on the wrong items, such as internal emails or orders below a threshold.
concepts.body:
A **filter** is a checkpoint inside a Zap. It looks at the data so far and asks a yes/no question. If the answer is yes, the run continues. If no, the run stops there and shows as **Filtered** in Zap history.

Each rule has three parts: a field, a condition, and a value. For example:

- `Order Total` (Number) Greater than `100`
- `Email` (Text) Does not contain `@mycompany.com`
- `Phone` Exists

Conditions come in types: text, number, date/time, true/false (boolean), and "exists / does not exist". Pick the type that matches the data. A number condition only works on values that really are numbers, and text conditions ignore upper and lower case.

You can combine rules with **AND** (all must be true) or **OR** (at least one must be true).

Where you place the filter matters. Put it as early as possible, right after the trigger if you can. Steps before the filter still run (and may use tasks); steps after it only run when it passes. The filter step itself does not use a task.

A filter can only stop a run. If you want different actions for different cases (urgent tickets to one channel, the rest to another), you need paths, the next lesson.

Watch out with line items: a filter does not remove individual items from a list. It decides whether the whole run continues.
takeaways: A filter continues or stops the whole run based on rules
Place filters early; the filter itself costs no task
Choose the condition type that matches the data
pitfalls: Using a Text condition like "greater than" on numbers, which compares them as words and gives odd results.

quiz.q: You only want to notify Slack about orders over 100. The filter fails on an order of 250. What's a likely cause?
options: The rule used a Text condition instead of a Number condition
quiz.explain: Number comparisons need a Number condition; text conditions don't compare values numerically.

concepts.name: Paths: branching logic
concepts.summary: Split a Zap into branches so different data takes different actions, with Fallback and Always-run options.
concepts.why: Paths let one Zap handle several cases instead of maintaining near-duplicate Zaps.
concepts.body:
A filter can only say "continue or stop". **Paths** let a Zap choose between several routes, like an "if this, do that; otherwise do something else" decision.

Adding a Paths step creates branches, starting with Path A and Path B. Each branch has its own rules (written exactly like filter rules) and its own actions. Example for new support tickets:

- Path A, rule `Priority` equals `High`: page the on-call person and post in #urgent.
- Path B, rule `Priority` equals `Low`: add to the weekly backlog sheet.

Each branch can use one of three rule types:

- **Custom rules**: run when the conditions match.
- **Always run**: run every time.
- **Fallback**: run only when no other branch in the group matched. Use it to catch the unexpected case instead of silently doing nothing.

A group can hold up to 10 branches, and you can put paths inside paths (up to 3 levels). If more than one branch matches, each matching branch runs. Branches run one after another, left to right, so a slow step such as a long Delay in Path A holds up Path B.

The Paths step itself does not use tasks; only the actions in the branches that run do.

Keep paths readable: name each branch ("High priority"), keep rules simple, and if a branch grows long, move its steps into a Sub-Zap.
takeaways: Paths = several rule-based branches in one Zap
Add a Fallback branch to handle data no rule matched
Branches run in order, left to right
pitfalls: Forgetting that several branches can match at once, so two different actions run for the same item.

quiz.q: Which branch type runs only when no other branch in its group matches?
quiz.explain: A Fallback branch is the "otherwise" route for data no other branch matched.

concepts.name: Formatter: clean up text, numbers and dates
concepts.summary: Use Formatter by Zapier to change data into the shape the next app needs: split names, fix dates, do maths, look up values.
concepts.why: Apps rarely agree on formats; Formatter fixes mismatches without code.
concepts.body:
Data from one app often arrives in a shape the next app won't accept. A date written "03/04/2026" when the CRM wants "2026-04-03". A full name when the mailing tool wants first and last name separately. **Formatter by Zapier** is a built-in step that converts data between steps.

It has four groups:

- **Text**: split text ("Ana Lopez" into "Ana" and "Lopez"), change capitalisation, find and replace, extract an email address or URL from a longer message, remove extra spaces.
- **Numbers**: format currency and phone numbers, do simple maths (add tax), run spreadsheet-style formulas.
- **Date / Time**: change a date's format, convert time zones, add or subtract time ("due date = today + 7 days").
- **Utilities**: lookup tables, line-item tools, pick a value from a list, import a CSV file (a simple spreadsheet saved as text).

A **lookup table** maps one value to another, like a small dictionary: product code `P-01` becomes "Coffee mug". You can also set a fallback value for codes not in the table.

After a Formatter step, map its **Output** field in later steps, not the original field. This is the most common mistake.

Formatter is predictable: the same input always gives the same output. For messy text that needs understanding ("what is this email about?"), use an AI step instead. For simple reshaping, Formatter is cheaper and more reliable.
takeaways: Formatter converts text, numbers, dates and lists between steps
Map the Formatter step's output, not the original field
Prefer Formatter over AI for predictable reshaping
pitfalls: Adding a Formatter step but still mapping the original, unformatted field in the next action.

quiz.q: Your CRM rejects dates like "03/04/2026". Which step is the best fit?
quiz.explain: Formatter's Date / Time actions convert a date into the format the CRM expects.

concepts.name: Delays and schedules
concepts.summary: Pause a Zap for a while or until a date, and start Zaps on a timetable with Schedule by Zapier.
concepts.why: Many processes depend on timing: follow-ups after three days, reports every Monday.
concepts.body:
Not every Zap should act instantly.

**Delay by Zapier** is an action that pauses the run. Options:

- **Delay For**: wait a set amount of time ("wait 3 days, then send the follow-up").
- **Delay Until**: wait until a specific date and time, which can be mapped from earlier data ("remind one hour before the appointment").
- **Delay After Queue**: space runs out so they happen one at a time with a gap, helpful when an app limits how many requests it accepts per minute.

While waiting, the run shows as delayed in Zap history. If you edit the Zap during the wait, check what the delayed runs will do when they resume.

**Schedule by Zapier** is a trigger that starts a Zap on a timetable: every hour, every day at 9:00, every Monday, or once a month. It doesn't need an event from another app. Use it for regular jobs: a daily summary of new leads, a weekly reminder, a monthly report.

Pair it with search actions: "every morning, find all rows where status is Open, then post a count in Slack".

Time zones matter for both. Check your account's time zone setting, and when a date comes from another app, check which time zone it uses. Formatter can convert time zones if needed.

Delay and Schedule are not available on every plan, so check yours if you don't see them.
takeaways: Delay For / Delay Until pause a run; Delay After Queue spaces runs out
Schedule by Zapier starts Zaps on a timetable
Check time zones whenever timing matters
pitfalls: Using a long Delay inside one path, which holds up the branches after it.

quiz.q: You need to email a customer exactly one day before their booking date (which comes from the trigger). Which option fits?
options: Delay Until, using a date computed from the booking date
quiz.explain: Delay Until waits for a specific, mapped date; Formatter can subtract one day from the booking date first.

concepts.name: Webhooks: connect apps Zapier doesn't list
concepts.summary: Start a Zap when any system sends data to a special web address, and send data out to other systems the same way.
concepts.why: Webhooks connect Zapier to in-house tools and apps without a ready-made Zapier integration.
concepts.body:
Some systems aren't in Zapier's app list: your company's own tool, a niche service. Many of them can still send or receive **webhooks**.

A webhook is an automatic message one system sends to a web address when something happens. Think of it as the system "phoning" a URL (web address) and reading out the data, usually as JSON like the example below. Your developer or the app's settings page just needs the address to call.

**Catching webhooks.** Choose the **Webhooks by Zapier** trigger and the **Catch Hook** event. Zapier gives you a unique URL. Paste that URL into the other system's webhook settings, make it send one test event, then test the trigger. The JSON fields become normal fields you can map.

- If the system sends a list of objects in one call, the Zap runs once per object.
- **Catch Raw Hook** passes the data through untouched, plus the headers (extra labels sent with the request), for special cases.

**Sending webhooks.** The Webhooks by Zapier actions (such as POST or GET) send a request to another system's address. This is how you call an **API** (a door a service opens for other programs) when no ready-made action exists. The service's documentation tells you the URL, the fields it expects and how to send its API key.

Treat your Catch Hook URL like a password: anyone who knows it can start your Zap. The URL can change if the Zap moves to another owner, so update the sender then.
takeaways: A webhook is a system calling a URL with data, usually JSON
Catch Hook gives your Zap a URL other systems can call
Webhook actions let you call APIs that have no Zapier integration
pitfalls: Sharing the Catch Hook URL publicly, which lets anyone trigger the Zap.

quiz.q: Your in-house billing tool can send webhooks but isn't in Zapier's app list. How do you start a Zap from it?
options: Use a Webhooks by Zapier Catch Hook trigger and give its URL to the billing tool
quiz.explain: Catch Hook creates a URL; when the billing tool calls it, the Zap runs with the sent data.

concepts.name: Zapier Tables: store data for your Zaps
concepts.summary: Keep records in Zapier Tables, read and write them from Zaps, and use them as a simple database or AI knowledge.
concepts.why: Many automations need memory: what was already processed, a list of approved customers, a status per request.
concepts.body:
A Zap forgets everything after each run. When you need to remember things, such as which leads were already contacted, use **Zapier Tables**: a simple database built into Zapier. A database is just an organised place to store records, like a spreadsheet designed for programs.

A table has **fields** (columns, each with a type such as text, number, date, true/false, or a link to a record in another table) and **records** (rows). You can create a table from scratch, import data, or let AI draft one.

Zaps work with tables like with any other app:

- Triggers such as "new record" or "updated record" start Zaps.
- Actions create, update and find records.

Tables add a few handy features:

- **Formula fields** compute values from other fields, like in a spreadsheet.
- **AI fields** fill a field using AI, such as a one-line summary of a long note.
- **Linked records** connect rows across tables, such as orders to customers.
- Deleted records go to a Trash you can restore from.

Tables can also act as a **knowledge source** for AI steps, so an AI step can look up your product list or policies.

Why not just use Google Sheets? You can, but Tables live inside Zapier, so they connect without extra app connections and work closely with Forms. For very large or business-critical data, a real database or your CRM may still be the right home.

Sharing and permissions are set per table.
takeaways: Tables give Zaps memory: records with typed fields
Zaps can trigger on, create, update and find table records
Formula fields, AI fields and linked records add spreadsheet-like power

quiz.q: You want to make sure a Zap never contacts the same lead twice. How can Tables help?
options: Store contacted leads in a table and search it before contacting
Tables delete duplicate emails in Gmail
quiz.explain: A table remembers past runs; a find-record step plus a filter skips leads already stored.

concepts.name: Forms (formerly Interfaces) and Chatbots
concepts.summary: Build simple forms and pages that save to Tables and start Zaps, and know where Zapier Chatbots fit.
concepts.why: Automations often need a front door where people submit requests; Forms give you one without a web developer.
concepts.body:
Many automations start with a person asking for something: a time-off request, an IT ticket, a quote request. **Zapier Forms** lets you build that front door yourself. This product was called **Interfaces** until 2026; you'll still see the old name in some help links and older tutorials, and existing projects kept working after the rename.

You can start a form from an AI prompt, from an existing table, or from a blank template. Then:

- Add and edit fields (name, email, dropdowns, file upload).
- Add **conditional logic** to show or hide fields based on earlier answers.
- Choose what happens on submit: show a message, redirect to another page, open another page, or run a Zap.
- Connect the form to a **table** so every submission is stored as a record.

The usual pattern is Form -> Table -> Zap: the form saves a record, and a Zap triggered by the new record routes it, notifies someone, or creates a task. Forms can also give people editing access to a table without giving them a Zapier login to the table itself.

Preview and test the form before sharing its link, and check its access settings (public, or only people you invite).

Zapier also offers **Chatbots**: a chat window you can put on a website that answers from your own knowledge sources and can trigger Zaps. Chatbots, Forms and Tables can all be shown together in Canvas to document a full process.
takeaways: Zapier Forms is the new name of Interfaces
A common pattern: Form saves to a Table, a Zap reacts to new records
Use conditional logic and access settings before sharing
pitfalls: Following an old Interfaces tutorial and not finding menus that were renamed.

quiz.q: What is the usual way to process each new form submission automatically?
options: Store it in a table and trigger a Zap on the new record (or run a Zap on submit)
quiz.explain: Forms can save to a table and/or run a Zap on submit, which then handles the request.

concepts.name: Copilot and Canvas: build and plan with AI
concepts.summary: Describe an automation in plain words and let Copilot build it, and map whole processes visually in Canvas.
concepts.why: Copilot speeds up building, and Canvas helps you see how many Zaps, tables and people fit together.
concepts.body:
**Copilot** is Zapier's built-in AI assistant for building. You describe what you want in plain language, for example "when a Typeform is submitted, add the person to HubSpot and post their company in #sales", and Copilot drafts the Zap: it picks apps, events and field mappings. It can also add or replace steps in an existing Zap, explain fields, and help troubleshoot errors.

Copilot works across products too: it can set up tables, design forms, and help with AI steps. It offers an auto-build mode and a mode that asks before each change, and it keeps checkpoints you can go back to. As of Oct 2026 it is in open beta, so features still change.

Treat Copilot's work like a colleague's draft: test every step, check each mapping, and read the filters.

**Canvas** is a whiteboard for whole processes. A process often spans several Zaps, tables, forms, chatbots and manual steps done by people. Canvas lets you draw it: steps, split paths, text notes and groups, linked to the real Zaps and tables. You can generate a first draft with AI by describing the process, then adjust it.

Uses:

- Plan before building, so you spot missing steps.
- Document a system for colleagues: pin the canvas to a folder.
- Collaborate: invite teammates to edit.

A good Canvas makes it obvious which Zap to open when something breaks.
takeaways: Copilot drafts and edits Zaps, tables and forms from plain-language requests
Always test what Copilot builds
Canvas maps a whole process, including manual steps, and links to real assets

quiz.q: Copilot built a Zap that looks right. What should you still do before publishing?
options: Test each step and check the field mappings
quiz.explain: AI can pick the wrong field or event; testing catches it before it touches real data.

concepts.name: Looping over lists and line items
concepts.summary: Run the same actions once per item in a list (order lines, comma-separated tags) with Looping by Zapier.
concepts.why: Orders, invoices and forms often contain lists; without a loop you can only act on the list as a whole.
concepts.body:
One trigger can carry a whole list. An order holds several products; a form answer holds several tags. Zapier calls such lists **line items**. A normal action receives the whole list at once (often joined with commas). When you need one action per item, such as one CRM product line per ordered product, use a **loop**.

A loop means "repeat these steps for each item". **Looping by Zapier** creates loops from:

- **Text**: split a value such as `red, green, blue` by a separator (a comma by default).
- **Line items**: one iteration per item in a list field. You can include several line-item fields together, such as product name and quantity.
- **Numbers**: a start and end value, for example 1 to 10.

Every step after the Looping step runs once per item. Things to know:

- Iterations run in parallel, not one after another, and each appears as its own run in Zap history.
- Steps after the loop use one task per iteration, so a 200-item loop with two steps uses 400 tasks. Put one-time steps before the loop.
- To run a step only once at the end, add a filter that passes only when the `loop_iteration_is_last` field is true.
- One Looping step per Zap, no loops inside loops, and a cap on iterations (500 by default).
- A test creates only the first iteration; a live run creates all of them.

Formatter's line-item tools help prepare lists before looping, for example turning text into line items.
takeaways: Looping runs later steps once per item in a list
Iterations run in parallel and each uses tasks
Use loop_iteration_is_last with a filter for a one-time final step
pitfalls: Mapping the preview loop values field, which exists in tests but not in live runs.

quiz.q: An order has 5 products and 2 steps come after the Looping step. Roughly how many tasks do those steps use?
quiz.explain: Each of the 2 steps runs once per item: 5 x 2 = 10 tasks.

concepts.name: Error handlers, replay and autoreplay
concepts.summary: Decide what a Zap does when a step fails: run an error-handler path, retry automatically, or replay runs by hand.
concepts.why: Apps go down and data is sometimes bad; a reliable Zap plans for failure instead of failing silently.
concepts.body:
Steps fail for ordinary reasons: the other app is down for a minute, a required field was empty, a connection expired. Zapier gives you three tools.

**Replay.** From Zap history you can replay an errored run, either only the failed steps or the entire run with the original trigger data. A full replay counts as a new run and uses tasks. Fix the cause first, otherwise the replay fails the same way. Big changes to the Zap's structure can prevent replaying older runs.

**Autoreplay** retries failed steps automatically a few times, which handles short outages. It is an account setting, and on some plans it can be overridden per Zap.

**Custom error handling.** On any action step you can add an **error handler**: a separate path that runs only when that step fails. The original steps sit under "Success" and the handler under "Error". In the handler you might post the app's error message (it can be mapped) to a Slack channel, log the item in a table for review, or try another app. A handled run shows as Stopped/Handled rather than Errored. Notes:

- Not on the trigger or on a Paths step itself (but on steps inside paths).
- One handler per step; handlers can contain paths and more handlers.
- Autoreplay is turned off for Zaps with handlers, and Zapier doesn't email you when a handler runs, so make the handler notify someone.

Also know: by default Zapier turns off a Zap that errors on almost every run over several days, and it emails you about errors. Read those emails.
takeaways: Replay re-runs failed runs after you fix the cause
Autoreplay retries short outages automatically
Error handlers give a failing step its own recovery path
pitfalls: Adding an error handler that swallows failures quietly, so nobody ever learns that orders were missed.

quiz.q: A CRM step sometimes fails on bad data, and you want each failure posted to #ops with the error message. What fits best?
options: Add an error handler on the CRM step that posts the error to Slack
quiz.explain: An error handler runs only when that step fails and can map the app's error message into a Slack message.

concepts.name: Sub-Zaps and Code steps
concepts.summary: Package reusable steps as Sub-Zaps that other Zaps call, and know when a small Code step is the right tool.
concepts.why: Reuse keeps many Zaps consistent, and a few lines of code can replace a tangle of Formatter steps.
concepts.body:
**Sub-Zaps** let several Zaps share one set of steps, like a recipe you refer to instead of copying. If five Zaps all "look up the customer in the CRM and the billing app and combine the details", build that once as a Sub-Zap.

A Sub-Zap has three parts:

- **Start a Sub-Zap** trigger: lists the inputs it expects, for example `email`. Write "required" in a name to make that input mandatory.
- Any actions you like.
- **Return from Sub-Zap** action: chooses the outputs to send back, such as `customer_id` and `plan`.

In a main Zap, the **Call a Sub-Zap** action picks the Sub-Zap, maps data into its inputs, and receives its outputs for later steps. Fix a bug in the Sub-Zap and every caller benefits. Sub-Zaps are still labelled beta.

**Code by Zapier** runs a short program written in JavaScript or Python (two programming languages) inside a Zap. Use it sparingly, for things built-in steps make awkward, such as complex text parsing or calculations. Data from earlier steps comes in through an **Input Data** list of named values, and whatever the code returns becomes fields for later steps. Copilot or an AI assistant can draft the code for you, but you need someone who can read it.

Limits: Code steps have short time limits, can't safely store secrets such as API keys in the code, and use UTC (the world standard clock, not your local time zone). The separate Zapier Functions product was retired in September 2026; Zapier points users to Code steps instead.
takeaways: Sub-Zaps = reusable steps with defined inputs and outputs
Call a Sub-Zap maps data in and receives results back
Use Code steps only where built-in steps get awkward; never paste secrets into code

quiz.q: Which step must every Sub-Zap end with to send results back to the calling Zap?
quiz.explain: Return from Sub-Zap defines the outputs that the caller receives.

concepts.name: AI steps with tools, knowledge and approvals
concepts.summary: Give an AI by Zapier step app actions, knowledge sources and web browsing, with approvals and task limits (this replaced Zapier Agents).
concepts.why: Tools let AI do real work across apps inside a Zap, and approvals keep risky actions under human control.
concepts.body:
A plain AI step only reads the text you give it. An AI step with **tools** can also act: look up a customer in the CRM, search your documents, read a web page, create a task. The model decides which tools to use and how often, then returns its output fields. This is what people mean by an **AI agent**: an AI that takes several steps on its own to reach a goal.

Background: Zapier used to sell agents as a separate product, **Zapier Agents**. In October 2026 it moved those abilities into the AI by Zapier step, so agent-style work now lives inside normal Zaps with triggers, filters, paths and Zap history. Old agents show a migration banner.

Under Settings, **Tools and Knowledge** offers:

- **App actions**: any Zapier action. For each of its fields you choose: a fixed or mapped value, let the AI pick from a list, let the AI decide from the prompt, or leave the field out. Fix whatever you can, so the AI has fewer chances to get it wrong.
- **Knowledge sources**: documents or data (for example a table or a Drive folder) the step can search.
- **Browse the web**: search and visit websites.

Safety controls:

- **Require approval before running**, per tool. The run pauses, you get an email and a pending approval, and you approve or reject after seeing the values. Turn it on for anything that creates, changes, deletes or sends.
- A **task limit per run** (75 by default) pauses runaway runs.

Tools need the stronger model tiers or your own AI key, and task use varies per run, so check Zap history. Preview shows which tools were used.
takeaways: Tools let an AI step act across apps; Zapier Agents now lives here
Fix field values where you can; let the AI decide only what it must
Require approval for tools that change or send data, and keep a task limit
pitfalls: Letting the AI fill the recipient field of a "send email" tool with no approval step.

quiz.q: Which setting makes an AI step pause for a human before a tool runs?
quiz.explain: The per-tool approval toggle pauses the run until someone approves or rejects the call.

quiz.q: What happened to the standalone Zapier Agents product in October 2026?
options: Its capabilities moved into the AI by Zapier step inside Zaps
quiz.explain: Zapier announced that Zapier Agents is now AI by Zapier, a step that runs inside any Zap.

concepts.name: Zapier MCP: let AI assistants use your apps
concepts.summary: Connect AI assistants such as Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor to Zapier MCP so they can run actions in your apps, with controls.
concepts.why: MCP turns Zapier's app catalogue into tools any compatible AI assistant can use, which is powerful and needs care.
concepts.body:
Zaps run when an event happens. Sometimes you instead want to ask an AI assistant, in a chat, to do something: "add this person to HubSpot and invite them to Thursday's call". **MCP** (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that lets AI assistants plug into outside tools in a common way. **Zapier MCP** makes Zapier's apps available as such tools.

How it works:

- Add Zapier as a connector in your AI client (the app you chat in, such as Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor) and sign in.
- Zapier sets up your MCP server (the place the assistant connects to) and enables actions for apps you've already connected. You can ask the assistant to enable more apps; it will prompt you to connect accounts as needed.
- When you ask for something, the assistant finds the right Zapier action, asks for missing details, and runs it.

Each successful tool call uses Zapier tasks (two per call at the time of writing; failed calls don't count). Actions are logged in your history.

Controls and risks:

- Your app passwords stay inside Zapier; the AI model never sees them.
- Enable only the apps and actions you need, and remove access when done. Company admins can turn MCP on or off and may need to approve the connector.
- Some setups use a **connection token** (a long secret link). Never share it: anyone with it can run your tools.
- The assistant follows instructions it reads, including text hidden in emails or web pages. Keep write and delete actions narrow and review what it did.

Workflows you repeat often are better turned into Zaps, which run without a chat.
takeaways: Zapier MCP exposes your connected apps as tools for MCP-compatible AI assistants
Enable only the actions you need; credentials stay in Zapier
Never share a connection token; review what the assistant did
pitfalls: Enabling every action of every app "just in case", giving the assistant far more power than the task needs.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of Zapier MCP?
options: To let AI assistants run Zapier app actions on request
quiz.explain: MCP lets compatible AI clients use your connected apps through Zapier's actions.

concepts.name: Teams, admin controls and security
concepts.summary: Run Zapier safely in a company: shared folders and connections, ownership, admin app controls, SSO, audit logs and data retention.
concepts.why: Automations quietly become business-critical; they need owners, access rules and an audit trail.
concepts.body:
In a company, Zaps outlive the person who built them. Plan for that from the start.

**Collaboration**

- Keep team Zaps in **shared folders** so colleagues can see and fix them.
- Use **shared app connections** or service accounts (accounts created for a system, not a person) for important Zaps, so nothing breaks when someone leaves.
- Transfer ownership of Zaps and tables before people leave. A Catch Hook URL changes when a Zap's owner changes, so update senders.
- Write a short description on each Zap and pin a Canvas to the folder as documentation.

**Admin controls** (mostly on Team and Enterprise accounts):

- **Roles and permissions**: who can build, who can only view.
- **App controls**: allow or block specific apps, for example forbid personal file-sharing apps.
- **SSO** (single sign-on: staff log in with the company login, such as Okta or Google Workspace) and automatic account setup and removal.
- **Audit log**: a record of who changed what.
- **Data retention**: how long run data is kept.
- AI and MCP access settings.

**Data safety**

- Zap history stores the data that passed through each step. Avoid sending sensitive data (health, card numbers) through Zaps unless your company approved it.
- Connections give Zapier the same power as the connected account; use accounts with the least access needed.
- Zapier publishes its security and compliance information (for example SOC 2, an independent security audit) for your security team to review.

A short internal rule list (naming, owners, approved apps) prevents most problems.
takeaways: Use shared folders and shared or service-account connections for team Zaps
Admins control roles, allowed apps, SSO, audit logs and retention
Zap history stores data, so keep sensitive data out unless approved

quiz.q: A critical Zap broke when its builder left the company. What would most likely have prevented this?
options: Building it with a shared or service-account connection in a shared folder
quiz.explain: Personal connections and private Zaps stop working or become invisible when the owner leaves.

concepts.name: Designing robust Zaps and when not to use Zapier
concepts.summary: Recognise the limits of Zapier (volume, timing, complex logic, sensitive data) and design around them or choose another tool.
concepts.why: Knowing the edges keeps you from building something fragile and expensive that a different tool would do better.
concepts.body:
Zapier is excellent for connecting business apps at moderate volume. It is not the best tool for everything.

**Design habits that keep Zaps robust**

- One Zap, one purpose. Use Sub-Zaps for shared logic.
- Make Zaps safe to re-run: search before creating, so a replay doesn't create duplicates.
- Filter early, so unneeded runs stop before using tasks.
- Give every important step a plan for failure (error handler or alert).
- Watch out for **Zap loops**: Zap A updates a row, which triggers Zap B, which updates the row again, which triggers Zap A. Use filters or a "processed" field to break the cycle.

**Signs you may need something else**

- **Very high volume**: tens of thousands of events a day, or loops over thousands of items, multiply task costs. A data pipeline tool (software built to move large amounts of data) or custom code can be cheaper.
- **Instant, two-way interaction**: a Catch Hook always replies "OK" immediately and can't send back a computed answer, so it's not a real-time API.
- **Heavy logic**: many nested paths, big data transformations and long Code steps get hard to test. A programmer-friendly tool (such as n8n, or a small program) may fit better.
- **Strict data rules**: if data must stay on your own servers, a cloud service may not be allowed; self-hosted tools (software you run on your own servers) exist for that.
- **Business-critical timing**: polling delays and app outages are normal; don't rely on second-level precision.

**AI-specific**: AI steps vary between runs and can be wrong. Keep a human approval or review on anything customer-facing until results are proven over time.
takeaways: Make Zaps re-runnable, filter early, and plan failures
Break Zap loops with filters or a processed flag
High volume, real-time APIs, heavy logic or strict data rules may need another tool
pitfalls: Two Zaps that update the same record and trigger each other forever.

quiz.q: Zap A triggers on "Updated Row" and updates the same row. What risk does this create?
options: A loop where the Zap keeps triggering itself
quiz.explain: Each update fires the trigger again; a filter on a processed field breaks the cycle.

quiz.q: Which situation most suggests a tool other than Zapier?
options: Posting new form entries to Slack
Processing 200,000 events a day with complex transformations
quiz.explain: Very high volume with heavy logic gets costly and hard to manage in Zaps; pipelines or code fit better.
